name: Canvas
first: A view that draws shapes, images, and text with code, all in one view, in place of a view for each thing it draws.

dependsOn.why: A canvas draws paths, by filling or stroking them in its context.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The constant `circle` is a path, as `path` is on the page of Path, and line 10 fills it.

dependsOn.why: A canvas takes the whole size it is proposed in the steps of layout, and draws in that size.

what.is: A `Canvas` is a view that draws with code. It calls its closure with a graphics context, which draws paths, images, and text, and with the size of the canvas. Everything it draws is part of one view, not a view for each thing.
what.afterExample: The canvas draws a row of four blue circles, one every 50 points, in the size it was given, 200 by 10. It is one view, with no view for each circle.
what.problem: A drawing of many small pieces, such as the dots of a chart or the stars of a sky, would need a view for each piece, and SwiftUI does work for every view. A canvas draws all the pieces with code inside one view.
what.how: Apple's documentation says that a canvas passes a graphics context to its closure, for drawing, and a size, for fitting the drawing. It also says that a canvas offers no taps and no accessibility for the pieces it draws, and can be faster for a complex drawing.

when.text: Use a canvas for a drawing of many pieces that the user does not tap one by one, such as a chart, a pattern, or a graph.
Don't use a canvas for pieces that the user taps, or that VoiceOver must read, such as buttons. Views give each piece taps and accessibility, and a canvas does not.

parts.name: The closure, lines 3 to 13
parts.text: The closure draws the canvas. Its parameter `size` is the size of the canvas, so the drawing can fit it, and its parameter `context` is the graphics context it draws in. SwiftUI calls it each time the canvas is drawn.

parts.name: The graphics context `context`, line 10
parts.text: A graphics context has methods that draw, such as `fill(_:with:)`, which fills a path with a color. Each call draws on the canvas, on top of what was drawn before it.

steps.text: Line 3 makes a `Canvas`, with the closure that draws it. Nothing is drawn yet.
Lines 14 to 16 make a renderer that proposes 200 by 10, and line 17 draws. The canvas takes the size proposed, and calls its closure with a context and that size. Line 4 prints {{size 200.0 10.0}}.

The loop on line 6 runs 4 times. Each time, lines 7 to 9 make a circle 10 points wide, 50 points further right than the last, and line 10 fills it blue. Line 11 prints {{dot at 0}}, {{dot at 50}}, {{dot at 100}}, and {{dot at 150}}.

end.text: The canvas drew four circles with code, inside one view, in the size it got.
